body:
Kasapreko Company Limited is assessing the demand and supply conditions for Good X to optimise its market strategy. An economic consultant has provided an estimate of the demand function:

$Q_x^d = 12 - 2P_x + 0.2P_y + 0.025M + 0.3A_x$

where $Q_x^d$ is quantity demanded of Good X, $P_x$ the price of Good X, $P_y$ the price of Good Y, $M$ consumer income and $A_x$ advertising expenditure. Current market conditions: selling price of Good X: GH¢20 per unit; price of competing product Good Y: GH¢15 per unit; advertising expenditure: 200 units; consumer income: GH¢1000.

(a) (i) How many units of Good X will consumers purchase? **[1 mark]** (ii) Determine whether Good X and Good Y are substitutes or complements. Explain. **[3 marks]** (iii) Analyse whether Good X is a normal or inferior good. Explain. **[3 marks]** (iv) Express the demand equation as a function of $P_x$. **[3 marks]**
(b) While Kasapreko is legally supplying Good X, a parallel market has emerged. The consultant estimates that the supply function is $Q_s = -2 + 3P_x$. (i) Determine the market equilibrium price and quantity. **[4 marks]** (ii) Illustrate this using a supply and demand diagram. **[2 marks]**
(c) Suppose the government seizes half of Kasapreko's supply to restrict unauthorized sales (hint: $Q_s/2$). Find the new equilibrium price and quantity. **[4 marks]**
answer:
**(a)** (i) $Q_x = 12 - 40 + 3 + 25 + 60 = $ **60 units**.
(ii) The coefficient on $P_y$ is **+0.2**: a higher price of Y raises demand for X, so they are **substitutes** (competing products).
(iii) The income coefficient is **+0.025**: demand rises with income, so X is a **normal good**.
(iv) $Q_x^d = 12 - 2P_x + 3 + 25 + 60 = $ **$100 - 2P_x$**.

**(b)** (i) $100 - 2P = -2 + 3P \Rightarrow 5P = 102 \Rightarrow P^* = $ **GH¢20.40**, $Q^* = $ **59.2**. (ii) Demand from $(0, 50)$ to $(100, 0)$ in $(Q, P)$; supply from $P = 0.67$ upward; they cross at $(59.2, 20.4)$.

**(c)** $Q_s = \tfrac12(-2 + 3P) = -1 + 1.5P$. $100 - 2P = -1 + 1.5P \Rightarrow 3.5P = 101 \Rightarrow P \approx$ **GH¢28.86**, $Q \approx$ **42.3**.

> [!answer]
> 60 units; substitutes; normal; $Q = 100 - 2P_x$; $P^* = 20.4$, $Q^* = 59.2$; after seizure $P \approx 28.86$, $Q \approx 42.3$.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Signs of coefficients classify goods; halving supply shifts/rotates supply left, raising price and lowering quantity.

## Simplified explanation

Plug in the numbers to get 60 units and the demand line 100 − 2P. Equilibrium is about GH¢20.40. If half the supply is seized, the price jumps to about GH¢28.86.

body:
Provide a brief distinction between these pairs of concepts:

(i) Positive and normative economics **[2 marks]**
(ii) Economic model and economic theory **[2 marks]**
(iii) Deductive and inductive methods **[2 marks]**
(iv) Opportunity cost and trade-off **[2 marks]**
answer:
**(i)** Positive economics deals with *what is* (testable facts and cause-effect claims); normative economics deals with *what ought to be* (value judgements).

**(ii)** An **economic theory** is a tested generalisation explaining how economic variables are related; an **economic model** is a simplified (verbal, graphical or mathematical) representation used to express and apply a theory.

**(iii)** **Deductive**: start from a theory/hypothesis and derive predictions to test against facts (general → specific). **Inductive**: start from observed facts and generalise to a principle (specific → general).

**(iv)** A **trade-off** is the act of giving up one thing to get another because of scarcity; **opportunity cost** is the value of the best alternative given up in that trade-off.

> [!answer]
> What is vs what ought to be; tested explanation vs simplified representation; theory → facts vs facts → theory; the act of sacrificing vs the value of the best alternative sacrificed.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These are the building blocks of economic method: separating facts from values, using models to express theories, combining induction and deduction, and measuring trade-offs as opportunity costs.

## Simplified explanation

Facts vs opinions; ideas vs the simple picture of them; theory-first vs facts-first; giving up vs the value of what's given up.
hint: Give one line for each side of each pair.

body:
The table below shows the possible production combinations of Soyabean (tons) and Groundnut (tons) for Ghana given its available resources.

| Combination | Soyabean (tons) | Groundnut (tons) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 100 | 0 |
| B | 80 | 20 |
| C | 50 | 40 |
| D | 20 | 60 |
| E | 0 | 70 |

The country faces a trade-off when shifting production between Soyabean and Groundnut, illustrating the Production Possibility Curve (PPC).

(i) What is the opportunity cost of moving from combination B to C in terms of Soyabean given up per additional ton of Groundnut produced? **[2 marks]**
(ii) Calculate the Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT) between Soyabean and Groundnut using the movement from C to D. **[2 marks]**
(iii) If technological advancement shifts the PPC outward by 20%, what will be the new maximum possible output of Soyabean and Groundnut? **[2 marks]**
(iv) If the country is producing at point C, but resources are underutilized, what economic changes can move it to the PPC, and what does this imply about efficiency? **[2 marks]**
(v) Using a well-labelled diagram, indicate a point at which Ghana would be efficient, inefficient and unattainable. **[4 marks]**
answer:
**(i)** B → C: soyabean 80 → 50 (−30), groundnut 20 → 40 (+20). Opportunity cost $= 30/20 = $ **1.5 tons of soyabean per ton of groundnut**.

**(ii)** C → D: soyabean −30, groundnut +20. $MRT = \Delta S/\Delta G = 30/20 = $ **1.5**.

**(iii)** Maximum soyabean $= 100 \times 1.2 = $ **120 tons**; maximum groundnut $= 70 \times 1.2 = $ **84 tons**.

**(iv)** If resources are under-utilised the economy is actually *inside* the PPC (below the C output). Reducing unemployment, bringing idle land into use, and improving efficiency (better management, least-cost methods, removing waste) move it **onto** the PPC. It implies the economy is currently **inefficient**; output of both crops can rise without any sacrifice.

**(v)** Diagram with soyabean on one axis and groundnut on the other: any point **on** the curve (e.g. B or C) is efficient; a point **inside** (e.g. 40 soyabean, 20 groundnut) is inefficient; a point **outside** (e.g. 90 soyabean, 50 groundnut) is unattainable.

> [!answer]
> 1.5 tons of soyabean per ton of groundnut; MRT = 1.5; new maxima 120 and 84 tons; moving to the PPC needs full employment/efficiency (currently inefficient); on = efficient, inside = inefficient, outside = unattainable.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The MRT is the absolute slope of the PPC. Here it rises from 1 (A→B) to 1.5 (B→C, C→D) to 2 (D→E), showing increasing opportunity cost (a bowed-out PPC).

## Simplified explanation

Each extra ton of groundnut between B and D costs 1.5 tons of soyabean. A 20% better technology lets Ghana make up to 120 tons of soyabean or 84 of groundnut.
hint: Opportunity cost = soyabean lost ÷ groundnut gained.

body:
The market for Chelsea Jersey at the University of Cape Coast stadium is as follows:

| Price (GHS) | Quantity demanded | Quantity supplied |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 4,000 | 2,000 |
| 40 | 2,000 | 2,000 |
| 60 | 1,000 | 2,000 |
| 80 | 500 | 2,000 |
| 100 | 200 | 2,000 |

(i) What is the equilibrium price and quantity? Depict the equilibrium using demand and supply curves. **[3 marks]**
(ii) What is unusual about the supply curve? **[1 mark]**
(iii) At what prices would a shortage occur? **[1 mark]**
(iv) At what prices would a surplus occur? **[1 mark]**
(v) Suppose that with new admission in 2026, the quantity demanded at each price will be 1,000 more. What will be the new equilibrium conditions? **[3 marks]**
(vi) Depict the initial and new equilibriums on the same graph. **[1 mark]**
answer:
**(i)** $Q_d = Q_s$ at **P = GHS 40, Q = 2,000**.

**(ii)** Quantity supplied is **fixed at 2,000** whatever the price: the supply curve is **vertical (perfectly inelastic)**, as for stadium seats/jerseys in fixed stock.

**(iii)** Shortage below GHS 40, i.e. at **GHS 20** (shortage of 2,000).

**(iv)** Surplus at **GHS 60, 80 and 100** (surpluses of 1,000, 1,500 and 1,800).

**(v)** New $Q_d$: 5,000, 3,000, 2,000, 1,500, 1,200. Equilibrium: **P = GHS 60, Q = 2,000**: price rises by GHS 20, quantity unchanged because supply is fixed.

**(vi)** Vertical supply at Q = 2,000; $D_1$ crosses it at P = 40; $D_2$ (shifted right by 1,000) crosses it at P = 60.

> [!answer]
> P = 40, Q = 2,000; vertical supply; shortage at 20; surplus at 60–100; new equilibrium P = 60, Q = 2,000.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

With perfectly inelastic supply, demand shifts change only price, not quantity; price acts purely as a rationing device.

## Simplified explanation

The market clears at GHS 40 with 2,000 jerseys. The number of jerseys never changes, so when more students arrive only the price goes up, to GHS 60.

body: Explain the difference between total fixed cost and sunk cost. Give examples of each.
answer:
**Total fixed cost** is the cost of fixed inputs that does not vary with output in the short run but is still being incurred and may be avoidable in the long run (e.g. monthly rent, insurance premiums, salaries of permanent staff). A **sunk cost** has already been incurred and **cannot be recovered** whatever the firm does (e.g. money spent on market research or a non-refundable licence fee, specialised equipment with no resale value). Fixed costs can become avoidable when contracts end; sunk costs are bygones and should be ignored in decisions.

> [!answer]
> TFC: ongoing, output-independent costs (rent); sunk cost: already spent and unrecoverable (past research).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Sunk costs are irrelevant to marginal decisions; fixed costs matter for long-run decisions (exit) but not for short-run output choice.

## Simplified explanation

Fixed costs are bills you keep paying whatever you produce; sunk costs are money already gone for good.

body: How can a consumer raise his total utility if the ratio of his marginal utility to the price for good A is greater than that of good B?
answer:
Since $MU_A/P_A > MU_B/P_B$, the last cedi spent on A yields more utility than the last cedi on B. The consumer should **buy more of A and less of B** (shift spending from B to A). As he does so, $MU_A$ falls and $MU_B$ rises (diminishing MU) until $MU_A/P_A = MU_B/P_B$, where total utility is maximised.

> [!answer]
> Reallocate spending from B to A until the MU-per-cedi ratios are equal.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This is the equi-marginal principle.

## Simplified explanation

A gives more satisfaction per cedi, so spend more on A.
hint: Move money to the higher MU per cedi.

body: The law of diminishing marginal product implies the law of increasing costs. Explain.
answer:
As more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs, its **marginal product falls**. Each extra unit of output then needs **more** of the variable input, so the **marginal cost** of output rises: $MC = \dfrac{w}{MP_L}$. Falling MP therefore means rising MC (and eventually rising AVC and ATC): increasing costs.

> [!answer]
> MC = w / MP: when MP falls, MC rises.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The cost curves are mirror images of the product curves: MC is lowest where MP is highest, AVC lowest where AP is highest.

## Simplified explanation

If each new worker adds less output, each extra unit of output costs more.

body: Why does the principle of consumer equilibrium imply that people would tend to buy more apples when the price of apples is reduced?
answer:
In equilibrium $MU_{apple}/P_{apple} = MU_{other}/P_{other}$. A fall in the price of apples raises $MU_{apple}/P_{apple}$ above the ratio for other goods, so the last cedi spent on apples now gives more utility. The consumer buys more apples, which lowers their MU (diminishing MU) until equality is restored at a larger quantity of apples: the law of demand.

> [!answer]
> A lower price raises MU per cedi of apples, so buy more until the ratios are equal again.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This derives the downward-sloping demand curve from utility maximisation.

## Simplified explanation

Cheaper apples give more satisfaction per cedi, so you buy more.
hint: What happens to MU/P when P falls?

body: Explain the underlying difference between economies of scale and increasing returns to scale.
answer:
**Increasing returns to scale** is a **physical/technical** relationship: increasing all inputs by a proportion raises output by a **larger** proportion (double inputs → more than double output). **Economies of scale** is a **cost** concept: **long-run average cost falls** as output expands. Increasing returns to scale is one cause of economies of scale, but economies can also come from lower input prices (bulk buying), cheaper finance or marketing even when returns to scale are constant.

> [!answer]
> Returns to scale = input–output (physical) relation; economies of scale = falling long-run average cost (which may also come from pecuniary savings).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

With constant input prices, increasing returns to scale imply economies of scale; pecuniary economies can exist without them.

## Simplified explanation

One is about how much output you get; the other is about how cheap each unit becomes.

body:
Suppose that you are the manager of Royal Farms, the producer of fresh chicken in the Cape Coast Metropolis. With appropriate diagrams, examine the likely effects of the following on the market price and quantity of your fresh chicken:

(a) The Government of Ghana (GoG) has increased the incomes of your clients by 40%. **[5 marks]**
(b) The GoG is implementing a policy that provides subsidies for poultry farmers. **[3 marks]**
(c) An outbreak of chicken respiratory disease which is also detrimental to human health. **[6 marks]**
answer:
**(a)** Fresh chicken is a **normal good**, so higher incomes **shift demand right**: equilibrium **price and quantity both rise**. (Diagram: $D_1 \to D_2$ along a fixed S.)

**(b)** Subsidies lower production costs: **supply shifts right**: **price falls, quantity rises**. (Diagram: $S_1 \to S_2$ along a fixed D.)

**(c)** Two effects: (1) consumers fear for their health, so **demand shifts left**; (2) birds die or are culled and costs rise, so **supply shifts left**. **Quantity falls** for certain; the **price effect is indeterminate**: it falls if the demand fall dominates (the usual outcome with a human health scare), rises if the supply fall dominates. (Diagram: both curves shift left.)

> [!answer]
> (a) P↑, Q↑; (b) P↓, Q↑; (c) Q↓, P ambiguous.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Classify each event as a demand shifter (income, tastes/health fears) or a supply shifter (costs, subsidies, disease losses), then compare equilibria. Simultaneous shifts leave one variable ambiguous.

## Simplified explanation

Richer clients buy more chicken (price up). Subsidies let farmers produce more (price down). A disease scares buyers and kills birds, so less chicken is sold.
hint: Which curve shifts in each case?

body:
You consult with an economist on your staff who has conducted research on the elasticities of public transportation. She reports that the estimated price elasticity of demand for the first few months after a price change is about −0.3, but that after several years it will be about −1.5.

(i) Explain why the estimated values for price elasticity of demand differ. **[2.5 marks]**
(ii) Compute what will happen to ridership and revenue over the next few months if you decide to raise fares by 5%. **[2.5 marks]**
(iii) Compute what will happen to ridership and revenue over the next few years if you decide to raise fares by 5%. **[2 marks]**
(iv) What happens to total revenue now and after several years if you choose to raise fares? **[3 marks]**
answer:
**(i)** Elasticity is larger in the **long run** because people need **time to adjust**: to find substitutes (buy a car, use a bicycle, carpool), change where they live or work, or change habits. In the short run they are locked into routines, so demand is inelastic.

**(ii)** Short run: ridership change $= -0.3 \times 5\% = $ **−1.5%**. Revenue change $\approx 5\% - 1.5\% = $ **+3.5%** (exactly $1.05 \times 0.985 - 1 = +3.4\%$).

**(iii)** Long run: ridership change $= -1.5 \times 5\% = $ **−7.5%**. Revenue change $\approx 5\% - 7.5\% = $ **−2.5%** (exactly $1.05 \times 0.925 - 1 = -2.9\%$).

**(iv)** Total revenue **rises at first** (inelastic demand) but **falls after several years** (elastic demand) as riders switch to alternatives.

> [!answer]
> Elasticity grows with time to adjust; short run: riders −1.5%, revenue ≈ +3.5%; long run: riders −7.5%, revenue ≈ −2.5% (≈ −2.9% exactly).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Time is a key determinant of elasticity. The total revenue test: TR rises with price when |E| < 1, falls when |E| > 1.

## Simplified explanation

At first people keep riding and you earn more; later many find other ways to travel, so you earn less.

body:
Assume that the price of commodity x, $P_x$, is 4, the price of commodity y, $P_y$, is 4.5, and income is GHS34.

(i) Complete the table below **[3 marks]**:

| Quantity | $TU_x$ | $TU_y$ | $MU_x$ | $MU_y$ | $MU_x/P_x$ | $MU_y/P_y$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 22 | 27 | 22 | 27 | 5.5 | |
| 2 | 42 | 51 | 20 | | | 5.3 |
| 3 | 60 | 72 | 18 | 21 | | |
| 4 | 76 | 90 | 16 | 18 | | |
| 5 | | | | | 3.5 | 3.3 |
| 6 | 102 | 117 | 12 | 12 | | |
| 7 | 112 | 126 | 10 | 9 | | |

(ii) Find the equilibrium consumption bundle for the two commodities. **[3 marks]**
(iii) Suppose the consumer expects his/her income to increase soon and he/she therefore decides to smoothen consumption by increasing current consumption of commodity y to 5 units. Does this constitute a new stable equilibrium? Why and why not? **[4 marks]**
answer:
**(i)**

| Q | $TU_x$ | $TU_y$ | $MU_x$ | $MU_y$ | $MU_x/4$ | $MU_y/4.5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 22 | 27 | 22 | 27 | 5.5 | 6.0 |
| 2 | 42 | 51 | 20 | 24 | 5.0 | 5.3 |
| 3 | 60 | 72 | 18 | 21 | 4.5 | 4.7 |
| 4 | 76 | 90 | 16 | 18 | 4.0 | 4.0 |
| 5 | 90 | 105 | 14 | 15 | 3.5 | 3.3 |
| 6 | 102 | 117 | 12 | 12 | 3.0 | 2.7 |
| 7 | 112 | 126 | 10 | 9 | 2.5 | 2.0 |

(Row 5: $MU_x = 3.5 \times 4 = 14$, so $TU_x = 76 + 14 = 90$ (check: $90 + 12 = 102$ ✓); $TU_y(5) = TU_y(6) - MU_y(6) = 117 - 12 = 105$, so $MU_y(5) = 105 - 90 = 15$ and $15/4.5 = 3.3$ ✓. Row 2: $MU_y = 51 - 27 = 24$.)

**(ii)** At **x = 4, y = 4**: $MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y = 4$ and spending $= 4(4) + 4.5(4) = 16 + 18 = 34$ = income ✓. TU $= 76 + 90 = 166$.

**(iii)** **No.** Current income is still GHS34. Buying 5 units of y costs 22.5, leaving 11.5 for at most 2 units of x: TU $= 42 + 105 = 147 < 166$, and the MU-per-cedi ratios are unequal (5.0 for x vs 3.3 for y), so the consumer would gain by switching back. Expected future income does not change today's budget constraint, so this is not a stable equilibrium (unless the consumer borrows against future income, which changes the budget).

> [!answer]
> Missing values: $TU_x(5) = 90$, $TU_y(5) = 105$, $MU_x(5) = 14$, $MU_y(2) = 24$, $MU_y(5) = 15$, etc.; equilibrium x = 4, y = 4 (ratios = 4, budget spent); 5 units of y is not an equilibrium.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Consumer equilibrium requires both $MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y$ and $P_xx + P_yy = M$. A deviation that violates either condition lowers utility, so the consumer has an incentive to move back.

## Simplified explanation

Fill the gaps from the given numbers. At 4 of each, each cedi gives the same satisfaction and the money is used up. Buying 5 y now leaves too little for x and lowers total satisfaction.
hint: MU = ΔTU; equilibrium where MU/P are equal and income is spent.

body:
A biscuit producing company has the following short-run total cost function:

$TC = 100 + 50Q - 12Q^2 + Q^3$

(printed as $+Q^2$ in the last term; read as the usual cubic $+Q^3$), where TC is total cost and Q is the level of output. Determine:

(i) the total fixed cost function **[2 marks]**
(ii) the total variable cost function **[2 marks]**
(iii) the average variable cost function **[2 marks]**
(iv) the marginal cost function **[2 marks]**
(v) the TC, ATC, AVC and MC when the firm produces 10 units of output. **[2 marks]**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

TFC is TC at Q = 0; TVC is the rest. MC is the derivative of TC. AVC is minimised at $Q = 6$ (AVC = 14 = MC), consistent with MC cutting AVC at its minimum. (If the last term really were $+Q^2$, TC would be $100 + 50Q - 11Q^2$, an unusual cost function with negative MC beyond Q ≈ 2.3, so the cubic is intended.)

## Simplified explanation

The 100 is fixed. Everything with Q is variable. Plug in Q = 10: total 400, average 40, average variable 30, marginal 110.

body:
The market demand and supply equations for a product are $Q_D = 300 - 3P$ and $Q_S = 100 + 5P$, where Q is quantity and P is price.

(a) What are the equilibrium price and quantity for this product?
(b) Suppose that an increase in consumer income resulted in the new demand equation $Q_D = 420 - 3P$. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity for this product?
(c) Suppose the government enacts legislation that imposes a price ceiling equivalent to the original equilibrium price. What is the result of this legislation?
answer:
**(a)** $300 - 3P = 100 + 5P \Rightarrow 8P = 200 \Rightarrow P^* = 25$, $Q^* = 225$.

**(b)** $420 - 3P = 100 + 5P \Rightarrow 8P = 320 \Rightarrow P = 40$, $Q = 300$.

**(c)** With the new demand and a ceiling at P = 25: $Q_D = 420 - 75 = 345$, $Q_S = 225$: a **shortage of 120 units**. The price cannot rise to 40, so queues, rationing and black markets are likely.

> [!answer]
> P = 25, Q = 225; after the income rise P = 40, Q = 300; ceiling at 25 → shortage of 120.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A ceiling at the old equilibrium becomes binding once demand rises, freezing the price below the new market-clearing level.

## Simplified explanation

The price would normally rise from 25 to 40, but the ceiling keeps it at 25, so buyers want 345 while sellers offer only 225.

body:
The demand function for a good is

$Q_x = 56.6 - 0.25P_x - 0.03M + 0.45P_s + 0.6N$

where $Q_x$ is the quantity demanded of good X per week, $P_x$ is the price of good X per unit, $M$ is the average weekly income, $P_s$ is the price of a competing good S and $N$ is the population in millions. Given values are $P = 65$, $M = 350$, $P_s = 60$ and $N = 24$.

(a) Calculate the price elasticity of demand.
(b) Calculate the weekly income elasticity of demand.
(c) Find out what would happen to (a) if N rose to 26.
(d) Explain why good X is an inferior good.
answer:
First, $Q_x = 56.6 - 16.25 - 10.5 + 27 + 14.4 = 71.25$.

**(a)** $E_p = -0.25 \times \dfrac{65}{71.25} \approx $ **−0.23** (inelastic).

**(b)** $E_M = -0.03 \times \dfrac{350}{71.25} \approx $ **−0.15**.

**(c)** $N = 26$: $Q_x = 71.25 + 0.6(2) = 72.45$; $E_p = -0.25 \times \dfrac{65}{72.45} \approx -0.22$: demand becomes slightly **less** elastic (a larger quantity base).

**(d)** The income coefficient is **negative** (−0.03), so the income elasticity is negative: a rise in income **reduces** demand for X, the definition of an inferior good.

> [!answer]
> $Q_x = 71.25$; $E_p \approx -0.23$; $E_M \approx -0.15$; with N = 26, $E_p \approx -0.22$; inferior because demand falls as income rises.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Point elasticity for a linear function: $E_Z = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial Z}\dfrac{Z}{Q}$. A population increase shifts demand right; at the same price, the larger Q lowers |E_p|.

## Simplified explanation

Plug in the numbers to get 71.25. Then each elasticity is the coefficient times the variable divided by 71.25. The minus sign on income means X is inferior.
hint: Compute Q first, then coefficient × (variable ÷ Q).

body:
Suppose that the cross-price elasticity of demand for good X is 2.5 and the price of good Y increases by 25%.

(a) What is the relationship between good X and good Y?
(b) How will the increase in the price of good Y affect sales of good X?
answer:
**(a)** The cross-price elasticity is **positive**, so X and Y are **substitutes** (strong ones, since 2.5 > 1).

**(b)** $\%\Delta Q_x = 2.5 \times 25\% = $ **+62.5%**: sales of X rise by 62.5%.

> [!answer]
> Substitutes; sales of X rise 62.5%.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

$E_{xy} = \%\Delta Q_x / \%\Delta P_y$. A large positive value means consumers switch strongly between the goods.

## Simplified explanation

When Y gets dearer, people switch to X, so X sales jump by 62.5%.

body:
(i) Using the Production Possibility Frontier (PPF), explain the three basic tenets of Economics. **[5 marks]**
(ii) Show (on a typical PPF) how increasing costs are implicit in the shape of the PPF. **[6 marks]**
(iii) If the principle of increasing costs did not hold, what shape would the PPF assume? With diagram(s), explain any one of these cases. **[7 marks]**
(iv) With an appropriate illustration, explain how the law of demand reflects the law of diminishing marginal utility. **[7 marks]**
answer:
**(i)** The PPF illustrates: **scarcity** (points outside the curve are unattainable with limited resources); **choice** (the economy must pick one point on the curve, deciding what to produce); **opportunity cost** (moving along the curve, more of one good means less of the other; the slope measures the cost).

**(ii)** On a concave (bowed-out) PPF, equal increases in good X (e.g. 0→1→2→3) require ever larger sacrifices of good Y (e.g. 1, 2, 4 units). The slope gets steeper moving right because resources suited to Y are increasingly transferred to X, where they are less productive.

**(iii)** Without increasing costs the PPF would be a **straight line** (constant opportunity cost: resources equally suited to both goods, slope constant) or **convex to the origin** (decreasing opportunity cost, e.g. strong economies of scale/specialisation, slope flattening). Example: a straight-line PPF from 10 units of X to 20 units of Y means every unit of X always costs 2 Y.

**(iv)** With diminishing MU, a consumer buys a good up to where $MU_X/P_X = MU_M$ (MU of money), i.e. $P_X = MU_X/MU_M$. Since MU falls as more is consumed, the consumer will buy additional units **only at a lower price**. Plotting the price the consumer is willing to pay against quantity gives a downward-sloping demand curve that mirrors the falling MU curve. Example: willing to pay ₵10, ₵8, ₵6 for the 1st, 2nd and 3rd drinks.

> [!answer]
> PPF shows scarcity, choice and opportunity cost; concavity = increasing cost; otherwise a straight line (constant cost) or convex (decreasing cost); diminishing MU → buy more only at lower prices → downward-sloping demand.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The shape of the PPF reflects how substitutable resources are between uses: perfectly substitutable → linear; specialised → concave. Marshall's derivation of demand from diminishing MU assumes constant MU of money.

## Simplified explanation

The PPF shows we can't have everything and must choose and give things up. The curve bulges because costs rise. Each extra unit pleases less, so people buy more only if it's cheaper.

body:
(i) Differentiate between fixed and variable inputs. Provide examples of each and explain how they impact production decisions. **[5 marks]**
(ii) What is the difference between explicit and implicit costs? Why is it important for firms to consider both when calculating economic profit? **[6 marks]**
(iii) Using a well-labelled diagram, explain the three stages of production. Discuss the significance of each stage in the decision-making process of a firm. **[7 marks]**
(iv) With the aid of a diagram, explain the relationship between Marginal Product (MP), Total Product (TP) and Average Product (AP). **[7 marks]**
answer:
**(i)** **Fixed inputs** cannot be changed in the short run (factory building, heavy machinery, land under lease). **Variable inputs** can be changed with output (labour, raw materials, fuel). In the short run the firm changes output only by varying variable inputs against fixed ones, so diminishing returns apply; in the long run all inputs are variable and the firm chooses its scale.

**(ii)** **Explicit costs**: money payments to outsiders (wages, rent, materials). **Implicit costs**: opportunity costs of the owner's own resources (forgone salary, forgone rent/interest on own capital). Economic profit = TR − explicit − implicit costs. Ignoring implicit costs overstates profit and can lead a firm to stay in an activity that earns less than the owner's resources could earn elsewhere.

**(iii)** Diagram of TP, AP, MP against labour. **Stage I**: from zero to maximum AP (MP > AP, AP rising): fixed input under-used, so the firm should expand. **Stage II**: from maximum AP to MP = 0 (AP and MP falling, MP ≥ 0): the **rational stage of production**. **Stage III**: MP < 0, TP falling: too much variable input; never rational.

**(iv)** MP is the slope of TP: when MP rises, TP rises at an increasing rate; when MP falls but is positive, TP rises at a decreasing rate; when MP = 0, TP is at its maximum; when MP < 0, TP falls. When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP < AP, AP falls; **MP cuts AP at AP's maximum**.

> [!answer]
> Fixed vs variable inputs; explicit vs implicit costs (economic profit needs both); Stages I/II/III with Stage II rational; MP is TP's slope and cuts AP at its maximum.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The production function's shape (increasing then diminishing returns) determines the shape of short-run cost curves. The marginal–average relationship ties MP to AP just as MC ties to AC.

## Simplified explanation

Some inputs are stuck in the short run. Hidden costs matter for real profit. Firms operate where output per worker is falling but extra workers still add something.
hint: Short run vs long run; accounting vs economic profit.

body: What is the difference between self-interest and selfishness?
answer:
**Self-interest** means pursuing whatever gives a person the greatest satisfaction given their own goals; those goals may include the welfare of family, friends or society (e.g. giving to charity because it makes you happy). **Selfishness** means caring only about oneself, regardless of the harm to others. Economics assumes self-interest, not selfishness.

> [!answer]
> Self-interest = pursuing one's own goals (which can include others' welfare); selfishness = disregarding others.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Rational choice theory only requires purposeful, consistent behaviour; preferences can be altruistic.

## Simplified explanation

Doing what you value isn't the same as ignoring others.

body: What do economists mean by individuals thinking at the margins?
answer:
Making decisions by comparing the **additional (marginal) benefit** and **additional (marginal) cost** of a small change, e.g. one more hour of study, one more unit of output, rather than all-or-nothing choices. Act if $MB > MC$; stop where $MB = MC$. Past (sunk) costs are ignored.

> [!answer]
> Comparing the extra benefit and extra cost of a little more or a little less of an activity.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Marginal analysis underlies consumer equilibrium ($MU/P$), profit maximisation ($MR = MC$) and efficient resource allocation ($MB = MC$).

## Simplified explanation

Ask whether one more is worth its extra cost.

body: You are trying to decide whether to take a vacation. Most of the costs of the vacation (airfare, hotel, and forgone wages) are measured in dollars, but the benefits of the vacation are psychological. How can you compare the benefits to the costs?
answer:
Convert the benefit into money terms by asking your **willingness to pay**: the maximum amount you would be willing to pay for the vacation (or the amount someone would have to pay you to give it up). Compare that dollar value with the full opportunity cost (airfare + hotel + forgone wages). Take the vacation if willingness to pay ≥ total cost.

> [!answer]
> Value the benefit by your willingness to pay and compare it with the full (explicit + implicit) cost.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Economists measure subjective benefits through revealed or stated willingness to pay; costs must include implicit opportunity costs such as forgone wages.

## Simplified explanation

Ask yourself the most you'd pay for the trip, then compare with what it really costs you.

body: Should an economic model describe reality exactly?
answer:
**No.** A model is a **simplification** that focuses on the key relationships relevant to a question and leaves out unnecessary detail. A model as complex as reality would be useless for understanding or prediction (like a map at a 1:1 scale). A good model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by how realistic every assumption is.

> [!answer]
> No: models simplify to highlight what matters; their value lies in explanation and prediction.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Abstraction and ceteris paribus assumptions make models tractable and testable (Friedman's 'as if' argument).

## Simplified explanation

A model is a simple map, not a photograph.
hint: A map is not the territory.

body: Explain any five principles of economics and how they affect our daily lives.
answer:
(Mankiw's principles; any five)
1. **People face trade-offs**: choosing to study tonight means less time with friends.
2. **The cost of something is what you give up to get it** (opportunity cost): going to university costs tuition plus forgone earnings.
3. **Rational people think at the margin**: you decide whether to eat one more plate or work one more hour by comparing extra benefit and cost.
4. **People respond to incentives**: higher fuel prices lead people to use public transport.
5. **Trade can make everyone better off**: specialising in what you do best and buying the rest.
6. **Markets are usually a good way to organise economic activity**; 7. **Governments can sometimes improve market outcomes**; 8. **A country's standard of living depends on its productivity**; 9. **Prices rise when government prints too much money**; 10. **Society faces a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.**

> [!answer]
> E.g. trade-offs, opportunity cost, thinking at the margin, incentives, gains from trade, each illustrated by everyday choices.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The principles group into how people make decisions (1–4), how people interact (5–7) and how the economy works as a whole (8–10).

## Simplified explanation

Everyday choices involve giving things up, comparing extra gains and costs, reacting to incentives and gaining from trade.

body: Use a production possibilities frontier to describe the idea of "efficiency."
answer:
An economy is **efficient** when it gets the most it can from its scarce resources: it is producing at a point **on** the PPF, where more of one good can be produced only by producing less of the other. A point **inside** the frontier is **inefficient**: resources are idle or misallocated, so more of both goods could be produced. Points outside are unattainable.

> [!answer]
> Efficient = on the PPF (no way to get more of one good without less of another); inside = inefficient.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Points on the PPF are productively efficient; which point on the PPF is best (allocative efficiency) depends on society's preferences.

## Simplified explanation

On the curve you're using everything well; inside, you're wasting resources.

answer:
**(a)** Money for the car cannot be spent on school fees, housing, holidays or savings; a new car may also mean higher insurance, versus the repair costs and unreliability of the old one.

**(b)** More on district education means less for health, roads or security, or higher taxes/borrowing (less private consumption now or later).

**(c)** Funds for the factory cannot go to research, marketing, paying dividends or reducing debt; expansion also carries risk versus the safety of current operations.

**(d)** Time spent preparing cannot be used for research, consulting, family or leisure; less preparation saves time but lowers teaching quality.

> [!answer]
> Each decision gives up alternative uses of limited money or time (other purchases/savings; other public spending or taxes; other investments; research/leisure).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Every decision under scarcity has an opportunity cost; identifying the alternatives is the first step in rational choice.

## Simplified explanation

Whatever you spend money or time on, you can't use it for something else.
hint: Limited money or time has other uses.

body:
Classify each of the following statements as positive or normative. Explain.

(a) Society faces a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
(b) The Bank of Ghana should reduce the rate of money growth.
(c) Society ought to require welfare recipients to look for jobs.
(d) Lower tax rates encourage more work and more savings.
answer:
**(a) Positive**: a testable claim about how the economy behaves (the Phillips curve).
**(b) Normative**: 'should' expresses a policy recommendation based on values.
**(c) Normative**: 'ought to' expresses a value judgement.
**(d) Positive**: a testable cause-and-effect claim about incentives.

> [!answer]
> (a) positive, (b) normative, (c) normative, (d) positive.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Positive statements can be confirmed or refuted with evidence; normative statements depend on values.

## Simplified explanation

Statements with 'should' or 'ought' are opinions (normative); the others can be checked.

body: State **True or False** and justify your choice: *Positive statements are expressions of value judgments.*
answer:
**False.** Positive statements are objective, testable statements about *what is*; it is **normative** statements that express value judgements.

> [!answer]
> False.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Normative statements contain words like 'should', 'ought', 'fair'.

## Simplified explanation

Opinions are normative, not positive.

body: State **True or False** and justify your choice: *Rational behaviour implies that everyone will make identical choices.*
answer:
**False.** Rational people pursue their own goals purposefully, but they have **different preferences, incomes, information and circumstances**, so they make different choices (e.g. one student chooses economics, another medicine).

> [!answer]
> False.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Rationality is about consistency between goals and choices, not about the goals themselves.

## Simplified explanation

Sensible people still want different things.

body: State **True or False** and justify your choice: *Choices are costly because we must give up other opportunities that we value.*
answer:
**True.** Because resources (money, time) are scarce, every choice sacrifices the next best alternative: its **opportunity cost**.

> [!answer]
> True.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Even 'free' choices cost the value of the alternative use of time.

## Simplified explanation

Choosing one thing means missing another.

body: State **True or False** and justify your choice: *Rationality implies that someone with a suspended driver's license would not drive.*
answer:
**False.** A rational person compares the expected **benefit** of driving with the expected **cost** (probability of being caught × penalty, plus other risks). If the benefit is judged larger, a rational person may drive anyway. Rationality does not mean obeying the law; it means acting purposefully on costs and benefits (which is why penalties and enforcement matter).

> [!answer]
> False: a rational person weighs expected benefits and costs.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The economics of crime (Becker) treats law-breaking as a response to expected costs and benefits.

## Simplified explanation

If the gain seems bigger than the risk, a rational person might still drive.

body: State **True or False** and justify your choice: *Economic theories do not abstract from the particular details of situations so they can better focus on every aspect of the behaviour to be explained.*
answer:
**False.** Economic theories **do abstract** from detail: they deliberately leave out less important aspects so as to focus on the **key** relationships. Trying to include every aspect would make theories unworkable.

> [!answer]
> False: theories abstract to focus on what matters.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Abstraction (with ceteris paribus) is what makes models tractable and testable.

## Simplified explanation

Theories leave out details on purpose.
